**(A)** Sticky pollens with rough surface

In entomophilous flowers the pollen grains are spiny and coated with a yellow sticky substance, the pollen-kit, so they cling to the body of a visiting insect. Large quantities of light, dry, smooth pollen are adaptations of wind-pollinated flowers, where most pollen is wasted in the air.

**(D)** Megaspore mother cell

The diploid megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides by meiosis to form a linear tetrad of haploid megaspores. The megaspore is already a product of meiosis and divides only by mitosis to form the embryo sac, while the integuments and nucellus are diploid tissues that divide by mitosis.

**(C)** Secondary nucleus and endosperm

The secondary nucleus is diploid (formed by fusion of two haploid polar nuclei), but after triple fusion with a male gamete it becomes the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, so the endosperm is 3n. Integuments and nucellus are both diploid, root tip and shoot tip are both diploid, and antipodals and synergids are both haploid cells of the embryo sac.

**(D)** Synergids

Six chromosomes is the haploid number when 2n = 12. Synergids are haploid cells of the embryo sac (female gametophyte), so they carry 6. Leaf cells and cotyledons are diploid (12), and the endosperm is triploid (18).

**(C)** polar nuclei and male gamete

The two polar nuclei fuse to form the diploid secondary nucleus, and in triple fusion the second male gamete fuses with it to give the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which divides to form the endosperm. Polar nuclei alone give only the secondary nucleus, and the male gamete that enters a synergid does not fuse with it.

**(D)** Pollen grain

Nucellus, embryo sac and micropyle are all parts of the ovule, the female structure. The pollen grain is the male gametophyte produced in the anther, so it is the odd one out.

**(C)** A - IV, B - I, C - V, D - II

After fertilization the ovule becomes the seed: the funiculus becomes the stalk of the seed, the scar marking its attachment becomes the hilum of the seed, the zygote develops into the embryo, and the inner integument becomes the thin inner seed coat, the tegmen (the outer integument gives the testa).

[Note: the chapter does not state that the funiculus becomes the stalk of the seed; standard biology gives this.]
